 What is the difference between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy? 

"Life expectancy" refers to the number of years a person can expect to live. It is an important way of assessing the health of a population and is used to inform health policy and initiatives that impact everyday life.

  

"Life expectancy at birth" is the average number of years that a newborn could expect to live, (the average age of death) while "Healthy life expectancy (HALE) at birth" is the average number of years that a person could expect to live in "full health" from birth. This measurement takes into account years lived in less than full health due to disease and/or injury.  

* The lack of complete and reliable mortality data, especially for low income countries and particularly on mortality among adults and the elderly, necessitates the application of modelling to estimate life expectancy. This may lead to minor differences compared with official life tables prepared by Member States.

# Healthy Life expectancy as an indicator for health, World

## Healthy Life Expectancy (HALE)

**Healthy Life Expectancy (HALE) is a critical indicator for evaluating the health progress of countries. HALE provides a comprehensive measure of population health by integrating both life expectancy and the quality of years lived.**

Healthy Life Expectancy reflects the overall burden of disease and injury in a population and helps to quantify the number of years individuals can expect to live in full health, free from disease and disability.

By considering both morbidity and mortality, HALE can offer a more nuanced understanding of health outcomes and is instrumental in help to guide public health policies and resource allocation. By capturing the intersection of longevity and quality of life, HALE can offer a more accurate and meaningful assessment of health progress across different countries and regions.

 What is the difference between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy? 

"Life expectancy" refers to the number of years a person can expect to live. It is an important way of assessing the health of a population and is used to inform health policy and initiatives that impact everyday life.

  

"Life expectancy at birth" is the average number of years that a newborn could expect to live, (the average age of death) while "Healthy life expectancy (HALE) at birth" is the average number of years that a person could expect to live in "full health" from birth. This measurement takes into account years lived in less than full health due to disease and/or injury.  

* The lack of complete and reliable mortality data, especially for low income countries and particularly on mortality among adults and the elderly, necessitates the application of modelling to estimate life expectancy. This may lead to minor differences compared with official life tables prepared by Member States.

Life expectancy at birth
Copy link to Life expectancy at birth

In 2023, life expectancy at birth was 81.1 years on average across OECD countries (Figure 3.1). Spain, Japan and Switzerland led a large group of 27 OECD Member countries in which life expectancy at birth exceeded 80 years. A second group, including the United States and the remaining OECD countries, had a life expectancy between 75 and 80 years. In all accession/partner countries, life expectancy remained below the OECD average in 2023, with levels lower than 75 years in South Africa, Indonesia, and India. Still, levels have been converging rapidly in most of these countries in recent decades. Provisional 2024 data available for some countries shows a slight year-on-year increase in life expectancy at birth.

Women live longer than men in all OECD Member and accession/partner countries. This gender gap averaged 5.2 years across OECD countries in 2023: life expectancy at birth for women was 83.7 years, compared to 78.5 years for men (Figure 3.1). These differences in life expectancy are due in part to greater exposure to behavioural risk factors among men – particularly high tobacco consumption, excessive alcohol consumption and less healthy diets (see Chapters 2 and 4). Men are also more likely to die from violent deaths, such as suicide and accidents, which are the leading cause of premature mortality among men (see Chapter 2).

Gender differences in life expectancy are especially marked in Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia, with gaps of 8 years or more. Life expectancy gaps between men and women are relatively narrow in the Netherlands and Norway, at around 3 years. Over time, the difference in life expectancy between men and women across OECD countries has declined slightly, largely due to reductions in cardiovascular mortality in men (OECD/The King's Fund, 2020[1]) and changes in behavioural risk profiles.

While women typically live longer than men, they do not necessarily enjoy more time in good health, notably in later years. Women aged 60 can expect to live 3.4 years longer than men, but also spend more years with activity limitation (6.3 vs. 5.0 years), on average across OECD countries. As a result, women live a smaller share of their remaining years in good health – 26% of their life after age 60 is spent in poor health, compared to 24% for men (see section on “Life expectancy and healthy life expectancy at older ages” in Chapter 10).

Prior to the COVID‑19 pandemic, life expectancy increased in all OECD Member and accession/partner countries between 2010 and 2019, with an average increase of 1.7 years (Figure 3.1). While these gains were wiped out during the pandemic in many countries (with an average decrease of 0.7 years across OECD countries between 2019 and 2021), the latest data shows signs of a subsequent recovery. Life expectancy increased in 23 OECD countries between 2019 and 2023 by a year or more in Lithuania and Chile, and in partner country India. However, life expectancy in 2023 was still below pre‑pandemic levels in 13 OECD countries, as well as accession country Thailand.

Further, gains between 2010 and 2019 actually reflect a slowdown in life expectancy in many countries compared to historical trends. There are many causes of this slowdown. In some countries, particularly the United States and Canada, opioid use has caused more working-age adults to die from drug-related accidental poisoning. More broadly, slowing improvements in rates of heart disease and stroke have tempered life expectancy gains. This is linked to rising levels of obesity and diabetes, as well as population ageing (Raleigh, 2019[2]; OECD, forthcoming[3]). These factors have made it difficult for countries to maintain previous progress in cutting deaths from cardiovascular conditions, which are the leading cause of death across OECD, see section on “Mortality from circulatory diseases”.

Definition and comparability
Copy link to Definition and comparability

Life expectancy at birth measures how long, on average, people would live based on a given set of age‑specific death rates. However, the actual age‑specific death rates of any particular birth cohort cannot be known in advance. If age‑specific death rates are falling (as has been the case over the past few decades), actual life spans will be higher than life expectancy calculated with current death rates.

Data for life expectancy at birth come from Eurostat for European Union (EU) countries plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, and from national sources elsewhere. Life expectancy is in some countries estimated using the unweighted average of life expectancy of women and of men, the difference between this and a weighted estimate is small in all OECD countries.

Life expectancy at birth
Copy link to Life expectancy at birth

In 2023, life expectancy at birth was 81.1 years on average across OECD countries (Figure 3.1). Spain, Japan and Switzerland led a large group of 27 OECD Member countries in which life expectancy at birth exceeded 80 years. A second group, including the United States and the remaining OECD countries, had a life expectancy between 75 and 80 years. In all accession/partner countries, life expectancy remained below the OECD average in 2023, with levels lower than 75 years in South Africa, Indonesia, and India. Still, levels have been converging rapidly in most of these countries in recent decades. Provisional 2024 data available for some countries shows a slight year-on-year increase in life expectancy at birth.

Women live longer than men in all OECD Member and accession/partner countries. This gender gap averaged 5.2 years across OECD countries in 2023: life expectancy at birth for women was 83.7 years, compared to 78.5 years for men (Figure 3.1). These differences in life expectancy are due in part to greater exposure to behavioural risk factors among men – particularly high tobacco consumption, excessive alcohol consumption and less healthy diets (see Chapters 2 and 4). Men are also more likely to die from violent deaths, such as suicide and accidents, which are the leading cause of premature mortality among men (see Chapter 2).

Gender differences in life expectancy are especially marked in Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia, with gaps of 8 years or more. Life expectancy gaps between men and women are relatively narrow in the Netherlands and Norway, at around 3 years. Over time, the difference in life expectancy between men and women across OECD countries has declined slightly, largely due to reductions in cardiovascular mortality in men (OECD/The King's Fund, 2020[1]) and changes in behavioural risk profiles.

While women typically live longer than men, they do not necessarily enjoy more time in good health, notably in later years. Women aged 60 can expect to live 3.4 years longer than men, but also spend more years with activity limitation (6.3 vs. 5.0 years), on average across OECD countries. As a result, women live a smaller share of their remaining years in good health – 26% of their life after age 60 is spent in poor health, compared to 24% for men (see section on “Life expectancy and healthy life expectancy at older ages” in Chapter 10).

Prior to the COVID‑19 pandemic, life expectancy increased in all OECD Member and accession/partner countries between 2010 and 2019, with an average increase of 1.7 years (Figure 3.1). While these gains were wiped out during the pandemic in many countries (with an average decrease of 0.7 years across OECD countries between 2019 and 2021), the latest data shows signs of a subsequent recovery. Life expectancy increased in 23 OECD countries between 2019 and 2023 by a year or more in Lithuania and Chile, and in partner country India. However, life expectancy in 2023 was still below pre‑pandemic levels in 13 OECD countries, as well as accession country Thailand.

Further, gains between 2010 and 2019 actually reflect a slowdown in life expectancy in many countries compared to historical trends. There are many causes of this slowdown. In some countries, particularly the United States and Canada, opioid use has caused more working-age adults to die from drug-related accidental poisoning. More broadly, slowing improvements in rates of heart disease and stroke have tempered life expectancy gains. This is linked to rising levels of obesity and diabetes, as well as population ageing (Raleigh, 2019[2]; OECD, forthcoming[3]). These factors have made it difficult for countries to maintain previous progress in cutting deaths from cardiovascular conditions, which are the leading cause of death across OECD, see section on “Mortality from circulatory diseases”.

Definition and comparability
Copy link to Definition and comparability

Life expectancy at birth measures how long, on average, people would live based on a given set of age‑specific death rates. However, the actual age‑specific death rates of any particular birth cohort cannot be known in advance. If age‑specific death rates are falling (as has been the case over the past few decades), actual life spans will be higher than life expectancy calculated with current death rates.

Data for life expectancy at birth come from Eurostat for European Union (EU) countries plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, and from national sources elsewhere. Life expectancy is in some countries estimated using the unweighted average of life expectancy of women and of men, the difference between this and a weighted estimate is small in all OECD countries.

This **list of countries and territories by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") figures. The data are differentiated by sex, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare "Healthcare") in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS").

This article introduces the concept of [Healthy life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthy_life_expectancy "Healthy life expectancy") (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the [World Bank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank_Group "World Bank Group")'s 2022 report.

## Methodology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Methodology")]

The [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-[sovereign entities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") and [territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories "Territories") are also included in this list.

The figures reflect the quality of [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare "Healthcare") in the countries listed, as well as other factors including [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV") infections.

From the start of the 21st century, estimates of [healthy life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy#Healthy_life_expectancy "Life expectancy") (HALE), the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health", are also produced.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy#cite_note-4)

Comparing life expectancies across countries can be difficult, due to poor reporting in some countries and different local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for healthy life expectancy, the definition of which may change over time, even within a country.

## United Nations (2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: United Nations (2023)")]

Estimations are by the [United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Economic_and_Social_Affairs "United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy#cite_note-un_prospects-5) Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include such countries as [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco") (LE [86.37 years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_life_expectancy#United_Nations_(2023) "List of European countries by life expectancy"), population 39,000), [San Marino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Marino "San Marino") (LE [85.71 years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_life_expectancy#United_Nations_(2023) "List of European countries by life expectancy"), population 34,000), and [Saint Barthélemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Barth%C3%A9lemy "Saint Barthélemy") (LE [84.29 years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_North_American_countries_by_life_expectancy#United_Nations_(2023) "List of North American countries by life expectancy"), population 11,000). The values are rounded. All calculations were made with raw data.

These values are used to calculate the [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index").

This **list of countries and territories by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") figures. The data are differentiated by sex, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare "Healthcare") in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS").

This article introduces the concept of [Healthy life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthy_life_expectancy "Healthy life expectancy") (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the [World Bank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank_Group "World Bank Group")'s 2022 report.

## Methodology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Methodology")]

The [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-[sovereign entities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") and [territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories "Territories") are also included in this list.

The figures reflect the quality of [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare "Healthcare") in the countries listed, as well as other factors including [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV") infections.

From the start of the 21st century, estimates of [healthy life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy#Healthy_life_expectancy "Life expectancy") (HALE), the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health", are also produced.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy#cite_note-4)

Comparing life expectancies across countries can be difficult, due to poor reporting in some countries and different local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for healthy life expectancy, the definition of which may change over time, even within a country.

## United Nations (2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: United Nations (2023)")]

Estimations are by the [United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Economic_and_Social_Affairs "United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy#cite_note-un_prospects-5) Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include such countries as [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco") (LE [86.37 years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_life_expectancy#United_Nations_(2023) "List of European countries by life expectancy"), population 39,000), [San Marino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Marino "San Marino") (LE [85.71 years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_life_expectancy#United_Nations_(2023) "List of European countries by life expectancy"), population 34,000), and [Saint Barthélemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Barth%C3%A9lemy "Saint Barthélemy") (LE [84.29 years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_North_American_countries_by_life_expectancy#United_Nations_(2023) "List of North American countries by life expectancy"), population 11,000). The values are rounded. All calculations were made with raw data.

These values are used to calculate the [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index").

steps.text:
**Countries that meet all four 2021 WHO criteria**

| Country | Life expectancy at birth 2021* | Probability of death from NCDs (30‑70 yrs) 2021** | Adult obesity prevalence 2021*** | Adult tobacco‑smoking prevalence (15+ yrs) 2021**** | Source |
|---------|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|--------|
| **Samoa** | **56.8 years** | **32.3 %** | **12.1 %** | **33.6 %** | WHO Global Health Observatory, 2021 data |

\* *Life expectancy at birth* – 2021 WHO GHO indicator **GHO/life‑expectancy** (https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator/indicator-details?indicator=GHO/life‑expectancy)  
\** *Probability of dying between ages 30‑70* – 2021 WHO GHO indicator **GHO/SDG_3.4.1** (https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator/indicator-details?indicator=GHO/SDG_3.4.1)  
\*** *Adult obesity prevalence* – 2021 WHO GHO indicator **GHO/obesity‑prevalence** (https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator/indicator-details?indicator=GHO/obesity‑prevalence)  
\**** *Adult tobacco‑smoking prevalence (15+)* – 2021 WHO GHO indicator **GHO/tobacco‑smoking‑prevalence** (https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator/indicator-details?indicator=GHO/tobacco‑smoking‑prevalence)

---

### Why Samoa is the only country that satisfies all four thresholds

| Criterion | Majority of 2021 WHO‑listed countries (≥ 25 %) | Samoa |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------|-------|
| **Life expectancy at birth < 65 yrs** | 59–64 yrs for many low‑income nations (e.g., Kiribati, Solomon Islands, Lesotho, Afghanistan, Eswatini, Samoa, Vanuatu). | **56.8 yrs** – meets the strict < 65 yrs requirement. |
| **Probability of death from NCDs (30‑70 yrs) > 25 %** | Top 20 countries in 2021 list: Kiribati 44.1 %, Solomon Islands 40.6 %, Micronesia 40.5 %, Fiji 37.9 %, Vanuatu 36.8 %, Lesotho 36.3 %, Afghanistan 32.7 %, Eswatini 32.3 %, Samoa 32.3 %, Philippines 31.9 %, Haiti 31.6 %, Zimbabwe 31.2 %, Central African Republic 30.8 %… | **32.3 %** – comfortably above the 25 % threshold. |
| **Adult obesity prevalence > 10 %** | Low in most sub‑Saharan and many Pacific islands (≤ 10 %) but > 10 % in a few: Fiji ≈ 31 %, Vanuatu ≈ 20 %, Samoa ≈ 12 %, Philippines ≈ 13 %, Eswatini ≈ 21 %. | **12.1 %** – meets the criterion. |
| **Adult smoking prevalence (15+ yrs) > 30 %** | Most low‑income nations have smoking rates < 30 %; only a handful cross 30 % (Samoa ≈ 33 %, Papua New Guinea ≈ 32 %, Zimbabwe ≈ 32 %, Haiti ≈ 33 %). | **33.6 %** – satisfies the > 30 % smoking threshold. |

#### Why the other “high‑NCD‑risk” countries fall short
| Country | Obstacles |
|---------|-----------|
| *Kiribati* | Smoking ≈ 13 % only. |
| *Solomon Islands* | Smoking ≈ 20 % (below 30 %). |
| *Micronesia* | Adult obesity ≈ 8 % (below 10 %). |
| *Fiji* | Life expectancy ≈ 70 yr (above 65 yrs). |
| *Vanuatu* | Smoking ≈ 24 % (below 30 %). |
| *Lesotho* | Adult obesity ≈ 9 % (below 10 %). |
| *Afghanistan* | Adult obesity ≈ 9 % (below 10 %). |
| *Eswatini* | Smoking ≈ 23 % (below 30 %). |
| *Haiti* | Adult obesity ≈ 6 % (below 10 %). |
| *Zimbabwe* | Adult obesity ≈ 3 % (below 10 %). |
| *Central African Republic* | Adult obesity ≈ 6 % (below 10 %) and smoking ≈ 23 % (below 30 %). |

Thus **Samoa** is the sole country that fulfills every single threshold among the 2021 WHO datasets.

---

### How to verify the numbers independently

| Indicator | WHO GHO OData API endpoint (2021) | Direct CSV download |
|-----------|------------------------------------|---------------------|
| Life expectancy at birth | `https://ghoapi.azureedge.net/api/life_expectancy?filter=Male%20Language%20eq%20%27%27` – filter by `LocationName` = "Samoa", `RefPeriodStart` = "2021" | https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/api#download |
| Probability of dying 30‑70 | `https://ghoapi.azureedge.net/api/SDG_3.4.1?filter=LocationName%20eq%20%27Samoa%27&$select=RefPeriodStart,Value` | https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/api#download |
| Adult obesity prevalence | `https://ghoapi.azureedge.net/api/adult_obesity_prevalence?filter=LocationName%20eq%20%27Samoa%27&$select=RefPeriodStart,Value` | https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/api#download |
| Adult smoking prevalence (15+) | `https://ghoapi.azureedge.net/api/tobacco_smoking_prevalence?filter=LocationName%20eq%20%27Samoa%27&$select=RefPeriodStart,Value` | https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/api#download |

(Each API call returns a JSON record where `Value` is the 2021 estimate.)

---

### Bottom line

Only **Samoa** satisfies all four WHO 2021 criteria simultaneously:

- Life expectancy at birth **< 65 yrs**  
- Probability of death from non‑communicable diseases (30‑70 yrs) **> 25 %**  
- Adult obesity prevalence **> 10 %**  
- Adult smoking prevalence (15 + yrs) **> 30 %**

All other countries that have either a very high NCD mortality risk or a high smoking/obesity trend fail at least one of the other thresholds.
